title: Why I Wrote “Stay Calm” | Dimensional
gist: David Booth uses his own family's story — $15,000 in cash found in his father's safe deposit box in 1985, over 15% of his Depression-scarred parents' net worth, versus the $1 million-plus it would have compounded to had it been invested from the end of World War II — to argue that non-participation in equity markets is a distribution and access problem, not a carelessness problem. He frames investing as ordinary decision-making under uncertainty and cites a free Dimensional documentary on YouTube passing 30 million views as evidence of a large underserved audience, with his book Stay Calm as the next step in reaching it.

themes.theme: Depression Scarring and the Cash Drag Bill

insights.claim: When David Booth's father died in 1985, the family safe deposit box held $15,000 in physical cash, representing more than 15% of everything his parents owned.
insights.speaker: David Booth, Founder and Chairman
insights.so_what: A concrete magnitude for household cash-hoarding among trauma-scarred savers — the same behavioral drag that shows up today in oversized money-market and savings balances that never rotate into risk assets.
insights.quote: Inside was $15,000 in cash, more than 15% of everything my parents had.
insights.locator: When my dad passed away in 1985

insights.claim: Having watched banks fail during the Depression, Booth's father needed cash physically visible and accessible rather than intermediated, which is presented as the direct cause of the family's decades-long avoidance of the stock market.
insights.speaker: David Booth, Founder and Chairman
insights.so_what: Crisis experience produces multi-decade allocation behavior, not a multi-quarter one; expect cohorts scarred by 2008 or 2022 to under-allocate to risk far longer than valuation models assume.
insights.quote: Dad grew up watching banks fail. He needed that cash where he could see it.
insights.locator: Dad grew up watching banks fail

insights.claim: Money left in cash from the end of World War II until 1985 would have exceeded $1 million had it instead been invested, according to Booth's account of his parents' foregone returns.
insights.speaker: David Booth, Founder and Chairman
insights.so_what: Quantifies the compounding penalty of a roughly forty-year cash allocation — the single most useful number for arguing an investor out of sitting in cash.
insights.quote: If they’d invested that money when my dad came home from World War II, it would have been worth more than $1 million by the time we opened that box.
insights.locator: If they’d invested that money when

themes.theme: Perceived Exclusivity as the Real Barrier

insights.claim: Households that stay out of markets do so because they believe investing is reserved for insiders and 'not for people like them,' a belief Booth traces to his own plainspoken Kansas parents.
insights.speaker: David Booth, Founder and Chairman
insights.so_what: The binding constraint on retail market participation is perceived social exclusion, not fees or product availability — relevant to anyone sizing the addressable market for advice and low-cost access.
insights.quote: In their minds, investing was for insiders. Not for people like them.
insights.locator: I grew up in Kansas with Depression-era parents

insights.claim: Booth explicitly rejects carelessness as the explanation for non-participation, attributing it instead to the fact that no one ever demonstrated that investing is neither as complicated nor as exclusive as it appears.
insights.speaker: David Booth, Founder and Chairman
insights.so_what: Reframes financial inclusion as an education-and-demonstration problem rather than a behavioral-defect problem, which changes what interventions are worth funding.
insights.quote: Not because they’re careless, but because no one ever showed them that this wasn’t as complicated or as exclusive as it looks.
insights.locator: There are a lot of people

insights.claim: Booth's core mental model defines investing as making decisions under uncertainty, and argues that this is the same skill people already exercise through every job change and every move, so prospective investors are more competent than they believe.
insights.speaker: David Booth, Founder and Chairman
insights.so_what: A reusable framing for onboarding hesitant capital: lower the perceived skill bar rather than promise better forecasts.
insights.quote: Investing is about making decisions under uncertainty. That’s most of what life is.
insights.locator: You already know more about investing

insights.claim: A documentary Dimensional produced and released free on YouTube, expected to reach only a small audience, has surpassed 30 million views.
insights.speaker: David Booth, Founder and Chairman
insights.so_what: Evidence that free long-form video is a viable top-of-funnel channel for asset managers at a scale no advertising budget would buy — watch whether peers copy the free-documentary playbook.
insights.quote: It now has more than 30 million views. That told me the people are out there.
insights.locator: A few years ago we made a documentary

insights.claim: Booth interprets the documentary's 30 million views as proof of a large audience of people losing sleep over their financial future who have never had access to these ideas, and positions his book Stay Calm: Learn to Embrace Uncertainty in Investing and Life as the next step in reaching them.
insights.speaker: David Booth, Founder and Chairman
insights.so_what: Signals that Dimensional's founder is spending institutional brand capital on mass-market education rather than institutional distribution — a bet on widening the retail funnel.
insights.quote: There are people losing sleep over their financial future who’ve never had access to these ideas. That’s what I’m trying to fix.
insights.locator: My new book is called Stay Calm

insights.claim: Booth compresses fifty years of professional experience into a three-part prescription: stay calm, stay invested, and let markets work for you.
insights.speaker: David Booth, Founder and Chairman
insights.so_what: The explicit doctrine is buy-and-hold market exposure over timing or stock selection — the behavioral case, not the analytical one, is what is being sold.
insights.quote: Stay calm, stay invested, and let markets work for you.
